nameStory: This mysterious orchid gets its 'spotted' name from the purple-red speckles that dance across its pale lip petal, like tiny droplets of wine on cream fabric. The 'coralroot' part comes from its underground stem system that branches and twists like ocean coral, though you'll never see this hidden treasure unless you dig (which you shouldn't do!).
description: Spotted coralroot is a ghostly orchid that rises from the forest floor without a single green leaf. Standing 8-20 inches tall, it looks more like a dried flower stalk than a living plant, with a reddish-brown stem topped by small orchid flowers. This leafless wonder gets all its nutrients from fungi in the soil rather than making its own food through photosynthesis like most plants.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small orchid flowers with three petals and three sepals, the lower lip petal distinctly spotted with purple-red dots on a whitish background. Each flower is about half an inch across and slightly fragrant.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Completely leafless plant rising 8-20 inches from the ground on a single reddish-brown to yellowish stem that feels firm and slightly waxy to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: No true leaves at all, just small brownish scales that wrap around the stem like tiny sheaths - these feel papery and dry when touched.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops small oval capsules that hang downward from the stem, eventually splitting to release thousands of dust-like seeds.

habitat: Look for spotted coralroot in rich, mature deciduous and mixed forests with deep leaf litter and humus-rich soil. It prefers shaded areas under maples, oaks, and birches where the soil stays consistently moist but well-draining, often on gentle slopes or in forest hollows.

seasonality.spring: Usually dormant and invisible underground, though very occasionally early shoots may emerge in late spring in warmer areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from June through August when the full flowering stalks emerge and display their spotted flowers - this is when they're most easily spotted and identified.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open to release seeds, while the stems begin to brown and wither away completely.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent above ground with no visible traces - the coral-like root system rests dormant in the soil until next summer.

funFact: Spotted coralroot is essentially a plant vampire - it has completely given up photosynthesis and instead steals all its nutrients from fungi, which in turn are connected to nearby trees, making this orchid an indirect parasite of the forest giants around it.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other coralroots, but spotted coralroot is the only one with distinctly spotted flowers. Northern coralroot has tiny yellowish flowers without spots, while autumn coralroot has even smaller flowers that barely open. Memory trick: 'Spotted coralroot has spots' - the other coralroots don't!
contextualKnowledge: Many people are surprised to learn this odd-looking plant is actually an orchid, part of the same family as tropical beauties sold in flower shops. The complete lack of green leaves makes it one of the most unusual wildflowers you'll encounter in New England forests.
compareHints: Spotted coralroot is much showier than its coralroot cousins, with larger flowers that actually open fully to display their distinctive spots. Northern coralroot is smaller overall with tiny pale yellow-green flowers, while autumn coralroot has the smallest flowers of all that often stay nearly closed. If you can clearly see spotted petals, you've found the spotted coralroot.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Northern coralroot is much paler and blooms earlier than spotted coralroot, which has obvious purple spots and reddish coloring.
Autumn coralroot is much smaller and more delicate than spotted coralroot, with tiny flowers that often don't open fully, and it blooms in fall rather than summer.
